Manmohan Singh asked Gurcharan Das to sell re­form for him

brief.head: Built for episode 100
brief.text: Amit Varma told a friend start­ing a pod­cast[[x3]] to think not of what lis­ten­ers find in episode one but what they can binge by episode hun­dred. {114-S01}

brief.head: Hello, the poor
brief.text: Every human wel­fare in­di­ca­tor tracks per capita GDP[[x4]] far more than re­dis­tri­bu­tion, Amit Varma noted. So when econ­o­mists talk GDP, he said, they are talk­ing about the poor. {114-C03}

brief.head: Twelve branches a year
brief.text: All for­eign banks in India to­gether could open twelve branches a year, Ajay Shah said, raised to eigh­teen in a sup­posed act of great lib­er­al­i­sa­tion. {114-S03}

brief.head: Pour the concrete
brief.text: A tar­iff cut can al­ways be re­versed[[x5]], Ajay Shah said. What stead­ies firms is a cred­i­ble team that ex­plains its logic[[x6]] and ad­mits prob­lems hon­estly. {114-C15}

brief.head: Whispers won’t do
brief.text: Whispering to a joint sec­re­tary changes lit­tle[[x7]][[x8]], Ajay Shah ar­gued. Policy shifts when new ideas change the cli­mate of opin­ion up­stream, as be­fore 1991. {114-C18}

thought.label: Thought for the day
thought.who: Ajay Shah, to every enthusiastic nationalist demanding an Indian CPU or LLM[[x9]]

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on India after the tariffs
lead.head: Mind the other two-thirds

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 114

body: Donald Trump’s tar­iffs on India came in two in­stal­ments: 25 per cent on ev­ery­thing but elec­tron­ics and pharma, then an­other 25 per cent, sup­pos­edly to pun­ish India for buy­ing Russian crude. Fifty per cent, Ajay Shah said, is “a lot and it’s a mess”.

So Shah and Amit Varma took up the ques­tion their au­di­ence kept ask­ing: what should India do? Varma promised an episode that was timely, but also a “first draft of his­tory” of a piv­otal mo­ment.

Shah’s an­swer, built on an essay he wrote with Vijay Kelkar, was a roadmap in three parts: deep trade agree­ments with the rest of the rich world, re­form at home, and hard-headed deal­ings with America and China.
## The best twenty years
The start­ing point was 1991 to 2011, when India’s GDP grew about four­fold[[x1]]. “That is sim­ply the big­gest shin­ing suc­cess in 5,000 years of Indian his­tory,” Shah said. {114-C01}
It came from abroad: tech­nol­ogy, knowl­edge, cap­i­tal and mar­kets, once the Indian state got out of the way.
Yet India never played in good faith, Shah said. Its of­fi­cials spoiled trade talks and its rules were un­fair to for­eign firms. The West in­dulged it, as­sum­ing India would grow up.
Right-wing pop­ulism has ended that pa­tience. “What we see with Trump today is to some ex­tent made in India,” he said. {114-C04}
## Beyond America

America, Shah pointed out, is only about a third of the trade of the ad­vanced economies. The rest, from Western Europe and Canada to Japan, Taiwan, South Korea and Australia, is rich, demo­cratic and still open.

Democracies keep treaties for five, ten or twenty years, the hori­zon firms need to in­vest. “The prob­lem in work­ing with au­thor­i­tar­ian coun­tries is that strong­men are un­trust­wor­thy,” he said.

So India should help found a new glob­al­i­sa­tion, built on deep trade agree­ments that bind mem­bers to fair play on reg­u­la­tion, in­tel­lec­tual prop­erty, cap­i­tal and for­eign firms. {114-C09} That means an end to third-worldism and to “500 red lines”.
At home the list is long: a clean GST and car­bon tax, re­formed reg­u­la­tors, work­ing courts and cities, an agri­cul­ture that is no longer a holy cow, and fi­nance that can fund big projects.

Shah also wants re­silience, not au­tarky: fis­cal pru­dence, an RBI de­voted only to in­fla­tion tar­get­ing, and a rupee that gen­uinely floats. “A float­ing ex­change rate is a shock ab­sorber,” he said. {114-C14}
## Pride, pes­simism and speed
With Trump and with Xi Jinping alike, Shah ar­gued, India must ne­go­ti­ate from ex­per­tise rather than pride. If flat­tery works on Trump, India should flat­ter.

Varma agreed, but con­fessed to pes­simism. Politicians, he feared, would an­swer a 50 per cent tar­iff with a 60 per cent one and pre­fer nar­ra­tive bat­tles to hard global work, while the op­po­si­tion op­poses for the sake of op­pos­ing.
His rem­edy is for peo­ple who agree to be vocal, as out­siders had to be in the 1990s when the re­form­ers in­side gov­ern­ment could not sell re­form them­selves.
Shah ended with a play­book for firms: treat America like an emerg­ing mar­ket, chase the rest of the rich world, and move fast. “The race will go to the nim­ble,” he said. {114-C19}
Varma found hope in that. Indian firms, he said, have long found their way around bad pol­icy. “We can ad­just, we can be nim­ble.”

second.label: The Red Sea
second.head: Not a tanker in sight
second.deck: A map of LNG tankers showed Ajay Shah how India’s route to Europe closed

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the empty Red Sea

body: Ajay Shah’s friend Ashima Sharma showed him a map of the world with each of its roughly 700 LNG tankers plot­ted as a dot. Not one was in the Red Sea. {114-S04}

The Houthis are chok­ing the route, Shah said, and some ships pay them ran­som to pass. {#ransom} Since 1945 the US Navy has run free­dom of nav­i­ga­tion op­er­a­tions around the world. This time, he said, it has stepped back.

For India that is a heavy blow. Its nat­u­ral mar­ket for goods is Europe, and the Suez Canal, which he dated to 1869[[x2]], is “the magic”: the short way there, in­stead of the long route round the Cape of Good Hope. {114-J14}

quote.text: And there was not a sin­gle tanker in the Red Sea. There is just such a mind blow­ing mo­ment for me.

third.head: A panipuri theory of risk

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the 85-year-old and the 12-year-old

body: At a con­fer­ence that Ajay Shah and Ila Patnaik or­gan­ised at NIPFP, a Chilean econ­o­mist ex­plained cap­i­tal ac­count con­vert­ibil­ity with two char­ac­ters. {114-S05}

One is an 85-year-old who never leaves the house or eats out, for fear of fall­ing sick. The other is a 12-year-old who flies out of the door, tum­bles on the ground, plays with frogs and eats pa­nipuri on the road­side. The child falls sick all the time, and bounces back. {#bounce}
Shah wants India to be the child. The re­flex­ive urge to hide be­hind a high fence, he said, comes from in­se­cu­rity. Resilience means tak­ing shocks and bounc­ing back.
India, he pointed out, has al­ready rolled with the 1991 cri­sis, the nu­clear tests, Y2K, the Asian cri­sis and 2008. {#overcame} “India is not in­fe­rior,” he said.

p2.title: What India should do
p2.deck: Ajay Shah’s roadmap for India after the tariffs, argued out with Amit Varma chapter by chapter

quote.text: And that is sim­ply the big­gest shin­ing suc­cess in 5,000 years of Indian his­tory.

photo.caption: Vijay Kelkar in 2008
photo.credit: Press Information Bureau, Government of India, GODL-India

box.title: Where the roadmap comes from
box.text: Ajay Shah and Vijay Kelkar wrote *Indian economic strategy in the new globalisation* for the LEAP blog, pulling to­gether col­umns by Sajjid Z Chinoy, TN Ninan, Rajeswari Sengupta, Mihir S Sharma and oth­ers into one co­her­ent ar­gu­ment. {114-R02}

sections.label: The good times
sections.head: Twenty years, four gifts
sections.caption: India’s best twenty years, 1991 to 2011
body: Between 1991 and 2011[[x10]], Ajay Shah said, India’s GDP grew about four­fold. To find a bet­ter twenty years, you would have to go back to Mohenjo-daro. {114-C01}
The gains came from the West once the Indian state took down its own bar­ri­ers. By the West he means lib­eral democ­ra­cies, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan in­cluded.

First came tech­nol­ogy: ma­chine tools, CPUs, op­er­at­ing sys­tems, fibre and the in­ter­net. Nobody de­manded an Indian CPU or a sub­sidised chip fab then, and Shah sees no need for an Indian LLM now. If Indians can help build a CPU, great; if not, buy other people’s. {114-C02}
## Knowledge walks out the gate

Next came knowl­edge, from Indians who stud­ied and, above all, worked abroad, and from for­eign firms in India. Shah has “no shame in say­ing that Hyundai knew more about how to make cars than Tata Motors”. Those who learned at Hyundai’s fac­tory went on to Tata Motors, an­cil­lary firms and EV projects. {114-S02}
Then fi­nance. Foreign cap­i­tal backed the new econ­omy be­fore Indian in­vestors woke up to it. “It was the for­eign­ers that made Infosys great,” he said. And fi­nally, mar­kets abroad.
~ Amit Varma drew the moral. Poverty is humanity’s de­fault state, and growth in those years lifted hun­dreds of mil­lions out of it, so get­ting pol­icy right is “a moral im­per­a­tive”.

quote.text: And that is sim­ply the big­gest shin­ing suc­cess in 5,000 years of Indian his­tory.

sections.label: India and America
sections.head: Newton’s law of trade
sections.caption: the gravity model of trade
body: Trade, Ajay Shah said, be­haves like Newton’s grav­i­ta­tion: it rises with the prod­uct of two countries’ GDPs and falls with the square of the dis­tance be­tween them. {114-C05}[[x11]]
That is bad news for goods bound for America. The United States is vast but fairly in­ward-looking, and it is the far­thest place India can ship to. From China or Japan, Los Angeles is a short hop.
Amit Varma drew his own con­clu­sion: the closer he and Shah get to each other, the more likely they are to hug. {114-J01}
## Weightless pho­tons

Services es­cape grav­ity[[x12]]. On fibre-optic ca­bles pho­tons fly, Shah said, cor­rect­ing him­self after a YouTube com­menter ac­cused him of al­ways say­ing elec­trons. Photons are weight­less, so California is not far. {114-J09}

Hence ser­vices ex­ports to America thrive while goods strug­gle. Of about $460 bil­lion in Indian goods ex­ports, around $85 bil­lion go to the US, and about $65 bil­lion face the 50 per cent tar­iff. {#exports}
~ That is about 15 per cent of goods ex­ports, Shah said. The dy­namic ac­tion is in ser­vices, which bring in about $370 bil­lion.

quote.text: the trade be­tween two coun­tries is pro­por­tional to the prod­uct of their two GDPs di­vided by the dis­tance be­tween them squared.

sections.label: The American wound
sections.head: A sound US is India’s business
sections.caption: why India needs a healthy America
body: Amit Varma is an anti-tariff ab­so­lutist. Tariffs, he said, are al­ways bad for your own peo­ple, which is why India should have none at all.
Ajay Shah agreed that America is hurt­ing it­self, though a once-in-a-century AI capex boom hides it. Split the Magnificent 7 from the rest of the S&P 500, he said, and the pain shows.

He listed the harms: ris­ing prices and unan­chored in­fla­tion; un­cer­tainty that chokes in­vest­ment and makes America “an emerg­ing mar­ket”; cost shocks for ex­porters re­liant on im­ported in­puts; and a fray­ing safe-haven dol­lar.

That mat­ters to India more than the tar­iff, he ar­gued. India needs American fi­nance, ser­vices de­mand, tech­nol­ogy, the GCCs built by American firms, and a US Navy that keeps the Red Sea open. {114-C06}
## Not a switch
Nor will the tar­iff switch off $65 bil­lion of ex­ports at a stroke, Shah said. {114-C07}

A $10 shirt hit by a 50 per cent tar­iff looks like game over. {#shirt} But Vietnam takes the American order and India picks up the German buyer Vietnam used to serve. The rupee falls, firms ab­sorb some mar­gin, and work­ers move to other em­ploy­ers.
~ Varma added Henry Hazlitt’s bro­ken win­dow: the ad­just­ments do not make the tar­iff harm­less, be­cause what is un­seen is what would have hap­pened with­out it. {114-R10}

quote.text: The world needs a sound United States. India needs a sound United States.

sections.label: A new globalisation
sections.head: Founders of a new club
sections.caption: deep trade agreements
body: America is only about a third of ad­vanced-economy trade, Ajay Shah said. India should em­brace the rest: Western Europe, Canada, Chile, Australia, New Zealand, Japan, Taiwan, South Korea and Israel.

They are rich, and they are democ­ra­cies, so a treaty signed with them holds for five, ten or twenty years. Strongmen rule by dis­cre­tion and change their minds overnight, and firms sim­ply wait and watch. {114-C08}

The WTO failed, he said, be­cause coun­tries could cheat. A deep trade agree­ment binds mem­bers[[x13]] to fair play on reg­u­la­tion, in­tel­lec­tual prop­erty, cap­i­tal and for­eign firms. The EU is one; the TPP, which eleven coun­tries pur­sued after Trump walked out, is an­other.
## No more third-worldism

India, Shah ar­gued, should help found a new coali­tion of ten or twenty like-minded coun­tries, and start up­grad­ing its trade agree­ment with the UK[[x14]] into a deep one now, since talks take two or three years. {114-C09}

That means drop­ping anti-colonial rhetoric and the habit of tor­pe­do­ing ne­go­ti­a­tions. Unfairness to for­eign­ers at home, he warned, feeds hos­tile pop­ulists abroad, who al­ready have a 20 per cent vote share in Germany. {#germany}

~ The prize could be con­crete: German car­mak­ers build­ing com­po­nents and soft­ware in India, Japanese elec­tron­ics firms pair­ing with Indian fac­to­ries, Korean ship­yards, and fru­gal de­fence part­ners in Ukraine, Poland and South Korea. {114-C11}

quote.text: India can and should be a founder mem­ber of a new glob­al­iza­tion.

sections.label: Reform at home
sections.head: Trade policy starts at home
sections.caption: domestic reform as trade policy
body: The sec­ond pil­lar of Ajay Shah’s plan is do­mes­tic, and each item, he said, ties back to win­ning the 66 per cent.

First, taxes. Non-residents are not India’s tax base, so ex­porters should get back every in­di­rect tax[[x15]] paid along the chain. India’s GST has “birth de­fects”, he said, and the world is con­verg­ing on a clean GST plus an au­ditable car­bon tax that meet at the bor­der. {114-C12}

Then reg­u­la­tors, who have be­come a new cen­tral plan­ning sys­tem; courts, so that penal­ties from for­eign buy­ers can be passed on to Indian ven­dors; and cities. A fac­tory of 20,000 work­ers on three shifts, he said, needs 60,000 house­holds nearby. {#shifts}
Agriculture can­not stay a holy cow. “Once we adopt red lines, you ba­si­cally stop doing diplo­macy,” Shah said. {114-C10}
## Trust as cur­rency
He wants re­silience, not au­tarky: fis­cal pru­dence, an RBI de­voted only to in­fla­tion tar­get­ing, a float­ing rupee and banks that don’t blow up.

Policy, he added, is an in­com­plete con­tract. A tar­iff cut can be re­versed, so cred­i­bil­ity comes from a vis­i­ble team that ex­plains its logic hon­estly, not a fatwa handed down like the Ten Commandments. {114-J18}
~ Foreign firms also need fair treat­ment, through OECD-style tax treaties and bi­lat­eral in­vest­ment treaties.

quote.text: The price of goods on a ship on the high seas should be minus Indian tax­a­tion.

sections.label: America and China
sections.head: Flatter, if flattery works
sections.caption: dealing with Trump and Xi Jinping
body: India can­not do au­tarky with the United States or with China, Ajay Shah said. It has to ne­go­ti­ate, and “there is no place for pride”.
With Trump, that means deep ex­per­tise on MAGA and the new American right. If flat­tery will get India past him, Shah said, India should flat­ter. {114-R22}

With China, slo­gans of friend­ship won’t do after Doklam and Galwan and Chinese over­pro­duc­tion. India needs a brains trust that can get in­side Xi Jinping’s mind and work out the car­rots and sticks.
Twitter one-liners, au­tarky and “strate­gic au­ton­omy”, he said, serve moral pu­rity, not the na­tional in­ter­est.
## Varma’s three wor­ries

Amit Varma agreed, and is pes­simistic all the same. Trade is never zero-sum, he said, yet the re­flex to an­swer a 50 per cent tar­iff with 60 per cent turns it into a game both sides lose. {114-C17}

Leaders, he feared, would pre­fer nar­ra­tive bat­tles, like the TikTok ban, to hard global work, and an op­po­si­tion that op­poses ev­ery­thing leaves no room for the cross-party states­man­ship of 1991 to 2011.
~ Shah’s an­swer was a the­ory of change: work up­stream of the pol­i­cy­maker, on ideas and the cli­mate of opin­ion. Varma cited Andrew Breitbart: pol­i­tics is down­stream of cul­ture. {114-J19}

quote.text: It is not a ques­tion of pride. It is a ques­tion of Indian self-interest.

portraits.caption: Xi Jinping
portraits.credit: Presidencia de la República del Ecuador, public domain

quote.text: Each of these points is di­rectly con­nected to the project of Indian deep glob­al­iza­tion so that we can do more with the sixty six so as to make up for the prob­lems of the thirty three.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: Vicks, Soviet factories, a stealthy reform and an argument over lunch

stories.kicker: Amit Varma retells a crisis at Richardson Vicks
stories.head: The rub that dodged a tax
body: Gurcharan Das was run­ning Richardson Vicks in India, around the early 1980s by Amit Varma’s reck­on­ing, when the gov­ern­ment slapped a new levy on cer­tain medicines. One of them was Vicks VapoRub, and the tax would make it un­prof­itable overnight.
Das called his top peo­ple to a cri­sis meet­ing. Then some­one in a cor­ner qui­etly pointed out two things. VapoRub’s for­mu­la­tion was com­pat­i­ble with Ayurveda. And Ayurveda was not taxed.

Within 24 hours the com­pany filed a pro­posal for an en­tirely new medicine, which was en­tirely the same medicine, now called an Ayurvedic rub. {#vicks24} The bu­reau­crat saw what they were up to, Varma said, but it was within the let­ter of the law, and it passed.
Das saw some­thing big­ger. As an Ayurvedic prod­uct, VapoRub could be sold at about four mil­lion out­lets, paan­walas in­cluded, in­stead of about 50,000 med­i­cal shops. {#outlets}

So he gave stock op­tions to every sin­gle per­son in the com­pany, down to the low­est peon. {#options} The com­pany reg­is­trar, who had never heard of stock op­tions, sus­pected a scam. Some staff could not af­ford Rs 20 a share, so the com­pany lent them the money.
If he re­mem­bered cor­rectly, Varma said, the share price rose forty times within a year, and every em­ployee made a down pay­ment on a house. {114-S09}
~ What did it tell him? “Indians do ju­gaad well,” Varma con­cluded, though he does not usu­ally cel­e­brate it.
stories.why: Indian firms can be re­mark­ably nim­ble under bad pol­icy. Firms should not have to re­sort to ju­gaad, Varma said, but the story gives him hope that Indian busi­ness can adapt to the tar­iff shock.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the Vicks VapoRub story

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s lesson for tariff-hit firms, from 1941
stories.head: Have factory, will travel
body: On 21 June 1941, Ajay Shah re­counted, the German army in­vaded the USSR[[x16]] and pushed about a thou­sand kilo­me­tres into Soviet ter­ri­tory, through the country’s in­dus­trial heart­land.
Under fire, the Soviets dis­man­tled en­tire fac­to­ries, car­ried them away to Central Asia, re­assem­bled them and restarted war pro­duc­tion. {114-S08}

“That’s how I feel today,” Shah said. If there is a 50 per cent tar­iff on India, dis­man­tle the fac­tory and take it to Sri Lanka. How dif­fi­cult is it, he asked, to put a whole fac­tory into a zero-tariff coun­try?
~ His point was about speed. In a fluc­tu­at­ing world, Indian firms that move faster than global ri­vals could find that nim­ble­ness is “a killer app”. {114-C19}
stories.why: In a world like this, a factory’s ad­dress is a choice, not a law of na­ture. Tariffs could swing to 300, Shah warned, and a Senate bill pro­poses sec­ondary oil tar­iffs of 500 per cent. {#senate}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the Soviet factories that moved

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on why the 1991 reforms needed salesmen
stories.head: Manmohan’s outsourced sales pitch
body: In the early 1990s, Amit Varma said, Gurcharan Das wrote to Manmohan Singh with a ques­tion: why are you doing re­forms by stealth?

Narasimha Rao and Manmohan Singh sold the re­forms as a bet­ter form of so­cial­ism that Nehru and Indira would have liked. They were re­ally a re­pu­di­a­tion of so­cial­ism, but the re­form­ers were scared of going against the party line and its he­roes. Deng Xiaoping and Margaret Thatcher, Das pointed out, sold their re­forms openly. {114-J21}
Manmohan Singh’s reply was short. “You come back and sell them for me.” {114-S07}

~ Naushad Forbes told Varma a sim­i­lar story. After a meet­ing of in­dus­tri­al­ists with Manmohan Singh, then fi­nance min­is­ter, Manmohan took Forbes aside: ev­ery­thing he had said in the meet­ing, he wanted said out­side. {#forbes}
stories.why: Reform needs pub­lic sales­man­ship, and in­sid­ers often can­not do it. That, Varma ar­gued, makes it the job of cit­i­zens and out­side voices: if you agree with these ideas, you can­not be a pas­sive ob­server.
stories.postscript: Varma’s episode with Montek Singh Ahluwalia, he said, traces how re­form­ers built these ideas from the late 1970s.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on reforms by stealth

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a lunch, a tariff and a Nobel nomination
stories.head: A bow too far for Nitin Pai
body: Just after the first 25 per cent tar­iff, Amit Varma had lunch with Nitin Pai, Narendra Shenoy and Sudhir Sarnobat.

The in­side dope, Varma said, was that Trump would not have im­posed the tar­iff if Modi had sim­ply agreed that Trump helped the peace process be­tween India and Pakistan. Pakistan had played along and nom­i­nated Trump for the Nobel Peace Prize.

Varma ar­gued Modi should kow­tow if he had to. “It’s not a mat­ter of ego or pride,” he said. “You just do what’s good for the coun­try.” The tar­iff, he said, hurt both Indians and Americans. {114-S06}
~ Pai was com­pletely against it, and the episode cut to a video of his re­ac­tion. But he “re­mains a friend”, Varma said. “We sur­vived that griev­ous in­ci­dent.” {114-J06}
stories.why: For Varma, the test of a leader is na­tional wel­fare, not na­tional ego. Pride is a cost cit­i­zens pay, which is also Ajay Shah’s case for choos­ing pros­per­ity over pride. {114-R22}

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 114. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Manmohan Singh (India, GODL-India); Vijay Kelkar (Press Information Bureau, Government of India, GODL-India); Donald Trump (Daniel Torok, public domain); Xi Jinping (Presidencia de la República del Ecuador, public domain); Gurcharan Das (Gurcharan Das, CC BY 3.0); Montek Singh Ahluwalia (Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0).

shelf.title: Indian economic strategy in the new globalisation
shelf.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: A sin­gle, co­her­ent roadmap for what India should do after the tar­iffs.

shelf.title: Recent columns on India’s response to the tariffs
shelf.creator: Sajjid Z Chinoy, Soham Das, TN Ninan, M Govinda Rao, Rajeswari Sengupta, Mihir S Sharma
shelf.why: He re­spects and val­ues their work as part of ‘one com­mu­nal sense of knowledge’ India is build­ing on this ques­tion.

shelf.title: The Globalisation Episode (EIE Ep 95)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ foun­da­tional think­ing on glob­al­i­sa­tion: first prin­ci­ples, a pot­ted in­tel­lec­tual his­tory up to the Second World War, and why tar­iffs harm a country’s own peo­ple and shift wealth from the poor to the rich.

shelf.title: Is Globalization Doomed? (EIE Ep 96)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The sec­ond part of the glob­al­i­sa­tion two-parter: how the open in­ter­na­tional order broke down, mainly be­cause China, and to a lesser ex­tent India, didn’t play by the rules, and why trade bar­ri­ers crip­ple man­u­fac­tur­ing.

shelf.title: Why Freedom Matters (EIE Ep 10)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Despite the title, an eco­nomic his­tory of India told through the lens of free­dom: the boom after 1869, Nehru’s Fabian so­cial­ism, the lost years from the 1962 war to the Emergency, and the open­ing-up that lifted mil­lions out of poverty.

shelf.title: How to Do Development (EIE Ep 57)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The case, built on Lant Pritchett’s ev­i­dence, that every human wel­fare in­di­ca­tor tracks per capita GDP, so sus­tained growth, not re­dis­tri­bu­tion or small solv­able projects, is the way out of poverty.

shelf.title: Caste & the Census (Seen/Unseen Ep 417)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: A timely de­bate on what count­ing caste in the cen­sus could do to Indian so­ci­ety.

shelf.title: What Just Happened Between India & Pakistan? (Seen/Unseen Ep 418)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: A con­ver­sa­tion recorded as events un­folded, with Pranay Kotasthane and Aditya Ramanathan, on the lat­est India-Pakistan clash, which showed both sides using fairly ad­vanced equip­ment.

shelf.title: Don’t Mess With the Price System (EIE Ep 66)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why the price sys­tem should be treated as sa­cred: price con­trols al­most al­ways lead to short­ages, and free prices let a shock work it­self out through many small ad­just­ments rather than one big col­lapse.

shelf.title: Economics in One Lesson (EIE Ep 109)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ episode on Hazlitt’s seen-versus-unseen lens, ap­plied to tar­iffs and gov­ern­ment spend­ing: you have to count what would have hap­pened with­out the in­ter­ven­tion.

shelf.title: Rules, Not Discretion (EIE Ep 92)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why a good so­ci­ety is built on rules rather than dis­cre­tionary power, which can’t an­chor long-term in­vest­ment, and why ex­perts should stay scep­ti­cal of their own ex­per­tise.

shelf.title: What Ails Indian Manufacturing? (EIE Ep 104)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s di­ag­no­sis of why Indian man­u­fac­tur­ing is weak: eight ways it dif­fers from ser­vices, twelve things that hob­ble it in India (from du­ties on im­ported in­puts to labour laws) and seven items for every state’s growth strat­egy.

shelf.title: Is Manufacturing the Answer? (EIE Ep 105)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The se­quel to What Ails Indian Manufacturing?, which dis­man­tles the myth of man­u­fac­tur­ing as un­skilled as­sem­bly-line labour.

shelf.title: Where Indian Regulation Went Wrong (EIE Ep 99)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s di­ag­no­sis of India’s statu­tory reg­u­la­tors as a new cen­tral plan­ning sys­tem that has to be fixed up­stream, at the level of or­gan­i­sa­tional de­sign, and of why fi­nan­cial reg­u­la­tors will never work per­fectly.

shelf.title: Why Talent Comes in Clusters (EIE Ep 8)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why the bright­est peo­ple con­cen­trate in places like Silicon Valley and Bell Labs, and how a clus­ter be­comes a mag­net for more tal­ent, helped by friendly reg­u­la­tion and a cul­ture where it is okay to fail.

shelf.title: What’s Wrong With Indian Agriculture? (EIE Ep 18)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why Indian farm­ing, which em­ploys 40 to 60% of Indians against about 5% in rich coun­tries, is held back by the lack of a work­ing price sys­tem: MSPs that favour ce­re­als over pulses, loan waivers in­stead of struc­tural re­form, gluts and col­laps­ing prices.

shelf.title: The Tragedy of Our Farm Bills (Seen/Unseen Ep 211)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Ajay and Amit on India’s farm bills, which would have kept APMCs but given farm­ers the choice to sell else­where, and on why farm re­form keeps stalling.

shelf.title: The Beauty of Finance (EIE Ep 21)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s mas­ter­class on why fi­nance ex­ists and why it mat­ters to the real econ­omy: fi­nance as ‘the brain of the economy’, not a casino for the rich, traced back to me­dieval trad­ing voy­ages.

shelf.title: What’s Wrong With the Indian Media? (EIE Ep 113)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Trusted in­for­ma­tion be­comes more valu­able, not less, in a world full of noise and mis­in­for­ma­tion.

shelf.title: The policy posture as an incomplete contract
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay ex­plains why no law truly pre-commits the state, since any law can be amended to­mor­row: re­forms stick only when an in­tel­lec­tual com­mu­nity, a cred­i­ble team and hon­est com­mu­ni­ca­tion stand be­hind them.

shelf.title: The Wonders of FDI (EIE Ep 111)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Fair treat­ment of for­eign firms, in­clud­ing pro­tec­tion against ex­pro­pri­a­tion, is part of deep in­te­gra­tion.

shelf.title: Great leaders choose prosperity over pride
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The core stance for ne­go­ti­at­ing with Trump: na­tional in­ter­est over ego.

shelf.title: The Importance of the 1991 Reforms (Seen/Unseen Ep 237)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Shruti Rajagopalan and Ajay on what 1991 achieved and left un­done (fac­tor mar­kets, agri­cul­ture), and how free­ing parts of the econ­omy set off the dis­cov­ery and trade be­hind India’s growth spurt.

shelf.title: The Reformers (EIE Ep 28)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The human story of the peo­ple who worked be­hind the scenes, often for decades and with­out re­ward, to open India up in 1991.

shelf.title: The Life and Times of Gurcharan Das (Seen/Unseen Ep 425)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Gurcharan Das
shelf.why: Gurcharan Das’s first-hand sto­ries of sell­ing re­form and of cor­po­rate nim­ble­ness; the con­ver­sa­tion led Amit to reread Sisyphus as a story about find­ing mean­ing in the act it­self rather than fu­til­ity.

shelf.title: Naushad Forbes Wants to Fix India (Seen/Unseen Ep 282)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Naushad Forbes
shelf.why: A busi­ness leader who backed re­form when there was al­most no pub­lic sup­port, show­ing that re­form­ers in­side gov­ern­ment needed out­siders to sell the ideas.

shelf.title: The Life and Times of Montek Singh Ahluwalia (Seen/Unseen Ep 285)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Montek Singh Ahluwalia
shelf.why: Montek Singh Ahluwalia’s first-hand ac­count of his decades in the re­form en­gine room and the ‘silent revolution’ that built up from the late 1970s.

shelf.title: The Long Road to Change (EIE Ep 36)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ the­ory of change: pol­icy im­proves through a decades-long pipe­line of data, re­search, rival pro­pos­als, pub­lic de­bate, com­mit­tee re­ports and draft laws, not by whis­per­ing in a joint secretary’s ear.

laughs.text: After Ajay ex­plains the grav­ity model, Amit con­cludes that ‘the closer Ajay and I get to each other, the more likely we are to hug.’ Ajay asks, ‘And will there be a hug­ging black hole?’ Amit backs off: ‘I’m not going to be get­ting into very dan­ger­ous things.’
Ajay of­fers a free T-shirt to who­ever binge-watches the most episodes in one week­end. Amit adds that the win­ner gets ‘that shirt which you’re wear­ing now, un­washed.’

Amit’s de­tour into ni­hilism: ‘No man is an is­land. Even though it must be said that every man is alone and will die re­al­iz­ing that life was mean­ing­less and any sense of pur­pose was a mere il­lu­sion... Forget about search­ing for the truth, set­tle for a good il­lu­sion.’

When Amit turns pes­simistic, Ajay says, ‘You em­body the mood of Bengali movies, but we should keep mak­ing more movies.’ Amit fires back that ‘you Gujaratis have a lot of re­spon­si­bil­ity for the state of the na­tion today, and I’m of course re­fer­ring to Gandhi and Patel.’
After re­count­ing his kow­tow­ing ar­gu­ment with Nitin Pai, Amit cuts to a video of Nitin’s re­ac­tion: he ‘re­mains a friend. We sur­vived that griev­ous in­ci­dent.’
Ajay imag­in­ing the West’s pa­tience with India: ‘As knowl­edge comes about in India, shows like EIE will come to India and the Indian side will grad­u­ally change.’
Amit’s trans­la­tion of the ‘tapestry’ of in­ter­linked episodes: ‘ta­pes­try is re­ally a fancy way of telling the gen­tle read­ers, binge watch, binge watch us.’
Ajay cor­rects him­self after a YouTube com­menter ac­cused him of al­ways say­ing elec­trons: on fibre optic ca­bles ‘it is pho­tons that fly,’ and they are weight­less.
Smoot-Hawley: Ajay says Trump’s tar­iffs are ‘un­heard of after Smoot-Hawley.’
‘We’re not in Kansas anymore’: Ajay’s line for how much the world has changed, and why India must re­think from scratch.
The Meiji Restoration: Japan sent a cou­ple of thou­sand young peo­ple West to study. Ajay says India’s flow of peo­ple abroad and back was far big­ger, and no­body made a fuss about it.
The Suez Canal and ‘the glory of 1869’: Ajay traces India’s nat­u­ral route to Europe via Gibraltar, the Mediterranean and the Red Sea, ver­sus the long way around the Cape of Good Hope.
The F-35: Ajay calls the American jet ‘com­pletely gold plated’ to ex­plain why fru­gal Ukrainian, Polish and South Korean de­fence part­ners suit India bet­ter.
The Ten Commandments: Ajay says that com­ing ‘down from the moun­tain with the ten commandments’ is worse pol­icy com­mu­ni­ca­tion than show­ing the full logic.
Andrew Breitbart’s ‘pol­i­tics is down­stream of culture’, quoted by Amit to ex­plain why think tanks tar­get­ing bu­reau­crats miss the point.

Deng Xiaoping and Margaret Thatcher: the lead­ers Gurcharan Das held up as re­form­ers who sold their ideas openly, un­like India’s sell­ing of re­form as a bet­ter so­cial­ism that ‘Nehru would have liked’.
